results.title: Dynamic Panel Data Estimation with System-GMM
results.content: While traditional static panel data models assume that idiosyncratic errors are uncorrelated across time periods, dynamic panel models account for temporal dependencies in the data by including the lagged dependent variable as a regressor, often providing a more accurate representation of economic relationships. ## Dynamic panel data model A general form of the dynamic panel data model is expressed as follows: Yit​=β1​Yi,t−1​+β2​xit​+uit​ * Yit​: Dependent variable for individual i at time t * Yi,t−1​: Lagged dependent variable * xit​: Vector of independent variables * uit​: Error term consisting of the unobserved individual-specific effect (μi​) and the idiosyncratic error (vit​) Key characteristics of the dynamic panel model: + *Dynamic dependent variable:* A lagged dependent variable is included among the regressors + *Endogenous explanatory (right-hand) variables* that are correlated with past and possible current error terms + *Fixed individual effects:* Unobserved heterogeneity among individuals, which is another source of persistence over time + *Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation* within individual units, but not across them Including the lagged dependent variable provides a more accurate representation of the dynamic nature of the data. ## Nickell bias As discovered by Nickell (1981), including the lagged dependent variable introduces endogeneity in the model due to its correlation with the error term. This transformation introduces a negative correlation between the transformed lagged dependent variable and the error term, resulting in a downward bias. It constructs valid instruments from both lagged levels and lagged differences of the endogenous variables, estimating a system of equations, one for each time period. Specifically, the following model is estimated: Empit​=β1​Empi,t−1​+β2​Wageit​+β3​Wagei,t−1​+β4​Capit​+β5​Capi,t−1​+μi​+vit​ - Empit​: Log of employment in firm i in year t - Independent variables include both current and lag values of log wages and log capital - μi​: Fixed effects per firm * The used instruments depend on assumptions about the correlation between the independent variables and the error term. # Load the package and data # Estimate the dynamic model with Two-step System GMM dyn_model <- pgmm(log(emp) ~ lag(log(emp), 1) + lag(log(wage), 0:1) + lag(log(capital), 0:1) | lag(log(emp), 2:99) + lag(log(wage), 2:99) + lag(log(capital), 2:99), * Lags of the endogenous variables are used as instruments, specified behind the `|`.

results.title: Nickell Bias in Panel Local Projection: Financial Crises Are Worse Than You Think†
results.content:
Title: Nickell Bias in Panel Local Projection: Financial Crises Are Worse Than You Think†
Panel local projection (LP) with fixed-effects (FE) estimation is widely adopted for evaluating the economic consequences of financial crises across countries. This paper highlights a fundamental methodological issue: the presence of the Nickell bias in the panel FE estimator due to inherent dynamic structures of panel predictive specifications, even if the regressors have no lagged dependent variables. We revisit four influential empirical studies on the impact of financial crises, and find that the FE method underestimates the economic losses of financial crises relative to the SPJ estimates. Despite its widespread adoption, the panel LP model is subject to a fundamental limitation: the FE estimator in panel LP inherently incurs the Nickell bias (Nickell, 1981), even in the absence of lagged dependent variables. It is a type of Nickell bias in the FE estimator for multiple-equation panel vector autoregression (VAR)—the full dynamic model behind. To eliminate the first-order Nickell bias and restore valid statistical inference in panel LP regressions, we propose the split-panel jackknife (SPJ) estimator (Dhaene and. Our paper makes econometric contributions to the literature on financial crises by highlighting the Nickell bias of FE in panel LP. The SPJ produces robust estimation and inference as in Section 2.4 even in this more complex setting with the lagged dependent variable and time fixed effects included in the regression. Saxena (2008), CS08 hereafter) in Section 3.4 ‣ 3 Revisiting the Aftermath of Financial Crises ‣ Nickell Bias in Panel Local Projection: Financial Crises Are Worse Than You Think†"), the number of cross-sections NN is larger than the time span TT. We use FE and SPJ to estimate the panel LP model (B11) over the replications. Among all methods for comparison, SPJ’s robustness remains under a variety of simulation settings, including the prototype model in Section C.1, panel LP with cross-sectional correlations as in Section C.2, penal LP with lagged dependent variable as in Section C.3, and some empirically oriented scenarios as in Section C.4 ‣ Appendix C Additional Simulation Results ‣ Nickell Bias in Panel Local Projection: Financial Crises Are Worse Than You Think†"). Even in the challenging setup with ρ\rho close to 1 as in Section C.5, SPJ still substantially mitigates the Nickell bias in FE.

results.content:
Title: Adding lagged dependent variables to differenced models
# Adding lagged dependent variables to differenced models. In sections 5.3-5.4, there is a great discussion of using. a lagged dependent variable with panel data. having trouble reconciling some of this discussion with a section in a. recent paper by Imbens and Wooldridge (2008) titled “Recent. their paper (as published by IZA in 2008) they suggest that it might. be better in some circumstances with two periods of data to use first. differencing and a lag of the dependent variable (assuming. of instrumenting for lagged variables if you have more than two. periods, but with two periods, how do you react to adding a lag (the. baseline value of the dependent variable) after first differencing. with only two periods of data? *The way I see it, once you add a lagged dependent variable to a differenced model, you are really doing lagged-dep-var control and not fixed effects. This is not always exactly true but it is a theorem for the simple example we use to contrast f.e. and lagged-dep-var control in Section 5.4*. the treatment, D\_it, is zero for everybody in period 1 and switched on for some in period 2 (think of a training program that some people participate in between periods; period 1 is before, period 2 is after (similar to Ashenfelter and Card, 1985)*. *ignoring constants,  fixed effects estimation fits*. *(1) Y\_it – Y\_it-1 = aD\_it + error*. *lagged dependent variable estimation fits*. *(2) Y\_it = gY\_it-1 + bD\_it + error*. *As I understand it, the Imbens-Wooldridge proposal is to throw Y\_it-1 into equation (1):*. *(3) Y\_it – Y\_it-1 = dY\_it-1 + cD\_it + error*. *But in this case, c is (algebraically) the same as b. *c= COV(Y\_it – Y\_it-1, D\_it\*)/V(D\_it\*)*. *where D\_it\* is the residual from a regression of D\_it on Y\_it-1. But this residual is orthogonal to Y\_it-1, hence*. *c= COV(Y\_it – Y\_it-1, D\_it\*)/V(D\_it\*) = COV(Y\_it, D\_it\*)/V(D\_it\*) = b in equation (2)*. *So I say: “You wanna do fixed effects? no lagged dependent variable, please (or at least be prepared to instrument it if you include one). Stack Overflow for Teams is now called **Stack Internal**. # Lagged variable(s) with random/fixed effects. I am running a regression on unbalanced panel data where I lagged by a timestep some of the explanatory variables. I also included an interaction effect between a lagged variable and a non-lagged variable. I wanted to ask if there is any possible problem that could arise that I need to be aware of while using a random/fixed effect model in the estimation. Thomas Bilach's user avatar. ## 2 Answers 2. Incorporating a lead and/or lag of your **in**dependent variable(s) in panel data contexts (e.g., fixed effects estimation) is generally not a problem. On the other hand, incorporating a lag of your *dependent* variable on the right-hand side of your equation will compromise consistency. The differenced/demeaned residual is necessarily correlated with your lagged outcome. Thus, feel free to adjust the time configuration of your **in**dependent variables as you see fit. Just be aware that it doesn’t necessarily absolve you of all endogeneity concerns. Thomas Bilach's user avatar. Please read , which makes Monte Carlo simulations to see what happens when you include a lagged dependend variable on the panel data regression. In short, you shoudn't use OLS, fixed effects or random effects in this case. Use Sys-GMM or D-GMM. Luiza Rodrigues's user avatar. ## Your Answer.
